rationale: Evidence from iteration 2 (60 dev trials per track set, 20 per track): widening the outer sensors to x = ±0.04 and lowering base_speed from 1.6 to 1.3 barely moved the result. Progress rose only from 0.11 to 0.115 on the oval and stayed at 0.15 on the s-bend, and slalom stayed at 0.105. Every run still ended off track with exactly one line-loss event, max_error stayed at about 0.062 m, and steering_oscillation stayed low (0.075 to 0.14). The failure point is therefore the same as before. The gain changes (iteration 1) and the sensor span change (iteration 2) did not move it, and the base_speed reduction only moved it slightly. Speed is the one lever not yet isolated. The evaluator's guidance for this result is to keep the ±0.04 sensors and lower base_speed further, to about 1.0. This isolates speed as the cause of the bend-entry line loss. I change only base_speed (1.3 to 1.0). Geometry, gains (kp 2.5, ki 0.3, kd 0.1), sensor weights and line_loss (last_direction) stay as in iteration 2, so any change in the result is attributable to speed. Expected result: if speed governs the failure, progress should rise clearly above 0.15 on the oval and s-bend, and line_loss_events should fall. Completion time will get much worse (the course needs about 1.5 m/s average to finish in 3 s, and 1.0 gives about 0.8 m/s), so this iteration is for finding the failure cause, not for completing. Hypotheses: (H3') the bend-entry line loss is caused by speed; if progress stays near 0.11 to 0.15 even at 1.0, speed is not the cause and the next suspects are the controller's turn authority (kp and the 350 PWM per turn scaling) and the line_loss recovery mode. Measurements wanted next: progress, line_loss_events and max_error per track, and whether the loss point moves along the course as speed changes.
